title: Palestinians in Gaza Are Lining Their Tents with Sandbags to Stop Israeli Bullets

Abu Adhra fortifies a side of his makeshift shelter with sandbags to protect
from Israeli gunfire, in the Bir 19 encampment in Khan Younis. November 18,
2026. Screenshot of video by Mohamed Ahmed.

_Story by Mohamed Ahmed and Sharif Abdel Kouddous_

KHAN YOUNIS, Gaza Strip--Nofal Al-Akhras filled another empty flour sack with
sand, tied off the top, and heaved it onto the other bags lining the outside
of his tent in the Bir 19 area of the southern Gaza Strip. A displacement camp
in a desolate sandy expanse west of Khan Younis, Bir 19 lies close to the
yellow line where occupying Israeli troops are stationed. Al-Akhras stacked
the sandbags three high, at about waist level, among drying laundry hung on a
sagging clothesline, forming a makeshift barrier--a desperate attempt to
protect himself and his family from Israeli gunfire.

"Every day, around the clock, we are caught off guard by stray, deadly bullets
fired indiscriminately," he told Drop Site News. "We have lost many loved ones
who were martyred by stray bullets striking displacement tents for no reason
whatsoever. We had no choice but to collect empty flour sacks, as you can see,
and fill them with sand to build protective barriers to shield our children,
our families, and our loved ones from the stray bullets."

Al-Akhras is not alone. Many families in Bir 19 have taken to placing sandbags
on the sides of their tents that face east toward the Israeli soldiers.
Palestinians in Gaza, already struggling to survive genocidal conditions
imposed by Israel--with multiple displacements, inadequate shelter, a lack of
protection from the winter cold, storms and flooding, shortages of food and
medicine, a lack of sanitation, and near daily aerial attacks--find themselves
having to crouch behind sandbags to avoid flying Israeli bullets.

Outside a nearby tent, a group of three children, no more than five or six
years old, stood holding open a large flour sack as an older boy slowly filled
it with shovelfuls of sand before struggling to stack it on some two dozen
others lining two sides of their tent. Inside another tent, several sandbags
were stacked at the head of each mattress. Two children lay on their backs
watching a video with their heads propped up on a pillow against the bulging
sacks.

###### Families use sacks filled with sand to protect their tents and shelters
from Israeli gunfire in Bir 19, Khan Younis on November 18, 2026. Video by
Mohamed Ahmed.

Many of the families in Bir 19 were displaced from Rafah, the southernmost
city in the Gaza Strip, which was invaded by the Israeli military in May 2024
and subsequently completely depopulated and razed to the ground.

"When the Israeli army entered Rafah, they ordered us to evacuate the city and
move to safe areas. We came to these 'safe areas' and settled here, but after
the Israeli army took control of Rafah, they began subjecting us to
indiscriminate gunfire every single day," Tareq Abu Adhra told Drop Site. He
worked with his daughter to fortify a line of sandbags outside his makeshift
shelter, made of tape and corrugated metal sheets.

"Every day, we hear bullets hitting the metal sheets and our tents. Our
neighbors have been wounded. A child was martyred, a young man was killed two
days ago, and a woman who was related to me was killed. Children are being
killed in schools," he added. "This is what life is like for us in Bir 19
every day. So we decided to build protective barriers to shield ourselves.
When we go to sleep at night, we sleep behind these barriers out of fear of
the gunfire."

Bir 19 camp residents pointed out multiple bullet holes in the sides of tents.
A sheet of corrugated metal at one makeshift shelter was riddled with bullet
holes. Another tent had a thick barrier built along one side using a patchwork
of rebar covered with tarp that was filled with sand about one meter thick.

"When we arrived here, we found that this was the worst place in the entire
Gaza Strip when it comes to stray gunfire," Abdul Rahman Abu Adhra told Drop
Site. "Just a week ago, a woman from our family was martyred when a bullet
struck her as she was walking. That's why we built these barriers, to protect
ourselves and our children."

"People just want to live. These are peaceful people but the Israelis aren't--
they won't leave anyone alone, not civilians, not women, not children, not the
elderly," he continued. "There's barely a kilometer between us and the
Israelis, and we're trapped between them and the sea. If they advance any
further, God help us. There will be nowhere left for us to go."

Israel has continued its near daily attacks despite a so-called ceasefire it
signed over a year ago, in October 2025. Since then, nearly 1,700 Palestinians
have been killed in airstrikes, shelling, and shootings by the Israeli
military. Israel has also steadily encroached further west in violation of the
agreement, moving from controlling 53% of the enclave to close to 70%, taking
over more Palestinian land and corralling the entirety of Gaza's population
onto less than a third of the territory. Many of the shootings occur close to
Israel's line of control, where Israeli troops are stationed alongside newly
built military bases.

On November 17, six-year-old Eyas Al-Namnam was shot and killed inside a tent
east of Deir al-Balah in central Gaza. According to his family, Eyas had just
woken up, started eating, and was doing his homework when his mother asked him
to go to his aunt's nearby tent to finish his work. He was accompanied by his
older brother and younger sister when Israeli forces opened fire.

"They hadn't even reached the entrance of the tent. His older brother went
inside and then his little sister. His cousin told his older brother to sit
down. His older brother sat down and Eyas was still standing. Then three shots
were fired at him. Two bullets struck the ground and one hit him in the
chest," another of Eyas's older brothers, Abdul Karim Al-Namnam, told Drop
Site just hours after the incident. He spoke standing in the morgue as Eyas's
small body wrapped in a white shroud and plastic body bag lay on a metal shelf
beside him. "We were displaced from Gaza City. We fled from the north to the
south, looking for safety. But there is no safety. There is no safety
anywhere. Ceasefire? What ceasefire? There is shooting twenty-four hours a
day. There is no peace at all. I wish there were some calm. At night, gunfire.
During the day, gunfire. In the afternoon, gunfire."

###### Family members mourn over the killing of six-year-old Eyas Al-Namnam,
who was shot and killed inside a tent east of Deir al-Balah on November 17,
2026. Footage by Mohamed Ahmed.

Abdul Karim had carried Eyas in his arms to Al-Aqsa Hospital. Doctors tried to
stop the bleeding for an hour and a half but were unable to resuscitate him.
"Eyas was a six-year-old boy, a beautiful boy with lovely curly black hair,
and he came in via the emergency department, the operating theater. He was
already very unstable," Dr. Mary O'Shea, an Irish anesthesiologist who was
volunteering at Al-Aqsa Hospital in Deir al-Balah for two weeks and was on the
scene, told Drop Site. "He had an obvious gunshot in the middle of his abdomen
and an exit wound at the back."

O'Shea said the hospital lacked the necessary equipment and medicines to
provide the best possible emergency medical care to Eyas. "Usually, in a big
trauma hospital, you get more information straight away--you would have scans,
you would have ultrasounds, you would be able to identify where the bleeding
was initially. You wouldn't be kind of searching in the dark," she said. "The
monitors in Gaza, they don't really work…and the drugs that we use are all out
of date, they're unreliable."

For the past three years, Gaza's health care system has come under sustained
attack by the Israeli military. Hospitals, clinics, and medical centers have
been bombed and raided, while a suffocating siege has caused severe
[shortages](https://www.dropsitenews.com/p/gaza-hospitals-medical-equipment-
supplies-israeli-blockade) of medicine as well as parts to repair and restore
critical equipment, bringing the healthcare system to the point of "systemic
collapse," according to the UN.

"That's one of the things that I've found hard to think about," O'Shea said.
"If he was somewhere else, would the outcome have been different? Maybe it
would have been. I can't say 100% if it would have been, but maybe--maybe we
would have been able to save Eyas's life, and that's heartbreaking. This is
the reality in Gaza. There's so many stories like this, so many stories."

In Bir 19, Manar Abu Adhra had one child killed by Israeli gunfire in a tent
earlier this year. Her daughter Rafif, just a year and five months old, was
ill, and Manar was preparing to take her to a clinic for treatment.

"It was around 7 a.m. I left her behind me in the tent and went outside to get
some clothes to change her into. Then I came back when I heard [her father]
screaming. A bullet had pierced her head while she was playing inside the
tent," Abu Adhra recalled. "She had done nothing wrong. She hadn't gone out to
fight. She wasn't part of the resistance or anything like that. She was just a
little girl inside her tent."

"We go to sleep afraid that we might lose another child, or that something
might happen to us adults," she added. "At night, we move the children into
this area so they can sleep behind the sand barriers we've built."

One of Abu Adhra's surviving children, eight-year-old Rahaf, hobbled beside
her on crutches as she spoke. Her right leg had been amputated just below the
waist after she was wounded in a separate Israeli attack.

"I lost my sister. Her name was Rafif. I lost her to stray gunfire, and we're
still suffering from the shooting to this day," Rahaf said. "I used to play
with her, and now I'm afraid to go to sleep because I might lose one of my
siblings or get shot myself. I just wish the war would end so we could finally
live without the constant gunfire."

_Jawa Ahmad contributed to this report. Khadija Abuyousif edited the video._
